\chapter{Asking Someone's Age}
\label{ch:ml-asking-age}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask how old someone is in Malayalam and answer with a dative subject.}

Ask ningaḷkku ethra vayassuṇṭŭ? and answer enikku irupatu vayassuṇṭŭ -- 'to me twenty age exists'.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ml{നിങ്ങൾക്ക്} \ml{എത്ര} \ml{വയസ്സുണ്ട്}?]{\ml{നിങ്ങൾക്ക്} \ml{എത്ര} \ml{വയസ്സുണ്ട്}? — \textquotedblleft{}to you, how much age exists?\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ML-C19-vayassu}



\begin{quote}
Same Sanskrit word as Kannada and Telugu — but Malayalam builds a genuinely different sentence around it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{വയസ്സ്}} (\emph{vayass}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{age}\textquotedblright{} — the same Sanskrit \textbf{\dv{वयस्}} (\emph{vayas}, \textquotedblleft{}age, vigor,\textquotedblright{} PIE cousin of Latin \textbf{vīs}) behind Kannada's \emph{vayassu} and Telugu's \emph{vayasu}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: dative subject + \textquotedblleft{}exists\textquotedblright{}}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{നിങ്ങൾക്ക്} \ml{എത്ര} \ml{വയസ്സുണ്ട്}?} — \textquotedblleft{}How old are you?\textquotedblright{} (formal/plural) — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to you, how much age exists}?\textquotedblright{} (\emph{ningaḷkku ethra vayassuṇṭŭ?} — from \emph{ningaḷkku}, \textquotedblleft{}to you\textquotedblright{} {[}dative{]} + \emph{ethra vayassu}, \textquotedblleft{}how much age\textquotedblright{} + \emph{uṇṭŭ}, \textquotedblleft{}exists.\textquotedblright{}) \textbf{\ml{എനിക്ക്} \ml{ഇരുപത്} \ml{വയസ്സുണ്ട്}.} — \textquotedblleft{}I am twenty years old.\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to me twenty age exists}.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{enikku irupatu vayassuṇṭŭ.})
\end{quote}

This is a real grammatical departure from Kannada and Telugu's plain \textquotedblleft{}your age how-much?\textquotedblright{} Malayalam puts the \textbf{person in the dative case} (\textquotedblleft{}to you,\textquotedblright{} not \textquotedblleft{}your\textquotedblright{}) and adds \textbf{\ml{ഉണ്ട്}} (\emph{uṇṭŭ}, \textquotedblleft{}exists, there is\textquotedblright{}) — the same existential verb Malayalam uses for ordinary possession and existence sentences generally. So the literal shape is \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to me, twenty years' worth of age exists}\textquotedblright{} — a dative-subject-plus-existential-verb construction, genuinely different from its two Dravidian cousins even though the age-word itself is identical.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vayassu\textquotedblright{} — age
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ningaḷkku ethra vayassuṇṭŭ?\textquotedblright{} — how old are you?
  \item \textquotedblleft{}enikku irupatu vayassuṇṭŭ\textquotedblright{} — I am twenty, \textquotedblleft{}to me twenty age exists\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is Malayalam's \textbf{\ml{വയസ്സ്}} the same Sanskrit word as Kannada's and Telugu's? (\textbf{Yes}.) Does Malayalam ask age the same simple way Kannada and Telugu do? (\textbf{No} — it uses a \textbf{dative} subject, \textquotedblleft{}to you,\textquotedblright{} plus the existential verb \textbf{\ml{ഉണ്ട്}}, \textquotedblleft{}exists.\textquotedblright{}) What does \emph{enikku irupatu vayassuṇṭŭ} literally mean? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{To me twenty age exists}.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
